title: A way of escape (1 Corinthians 10)
hookLine: no temptation beyond what you can bear, and the way out comes with it
tomorrow: what happens when a church dinner splits into full and hungry?

lines: A WAY OUT, WITH THE TEMPTATION.
cards: Midnight. A reply typed out, thumb over send, and you already know you'll regret it. Here's an odd detail in what Paul says about moments like that.
He promises a way out, and then he says when it shows up: "with the temptation." Not after the feeling passes, not once you've calmed down. With it.
Why would the exit come packed inside the trap?

teach.b: First the warning. Paul retells Israel's wilderness years as family history, "all our fathers," and says those things "are written for our admonition."
Then, to a church that feels very secure: "Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall."

Then the comfort, in one long sentence: "There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it."
Three promises in it. You're not the first; it's common to man. It won't be beyond what you're able.
And there's a door. Now the puzzle.
The door comes with the temptation because that's when it's needed; an exit that waited until the pull was gone would help nobody. And look at what it's for: "that ye may be able to bear it."
Some readers hear a way through, as much as a way out. Then Paul shows a door in use: "Wherefore, my dearly beloved, flee from idolatry." Flee.
Sometimes the exit is plain: stand up, leave the room.
One to tell a friend tonight: the popular saying is that God never gives you more than you can handle. Paul's line is narrower. It's about temptation, and what it promises is a door.

how: Some Christians memorize 1 Corinthians 10:13 and turn to it in times of temptation, praying it as a promise when a familiar pull comes back.

games.q: what does “a way of escape” mean?
o: a door God makes alongside the temptation
a promise you'll never face hard times
a rule to avoid every risky situation

games.q: a way of escape — tap the pairs.
p: not above that ye are able

s: the Bible says God never gives you more than you can handle
1 Corinthians 10:13 is about temptation, and what it promises is a way to escape.
Paul says the way of escape comes with the temptation
will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.
Paul says only the weak need to watch out
his warning goes to the confident: let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.

games.q: your brother keeps losing his temper during online games and wants to stop. what would Paul's way of escape look like?
o: catch the moment it starts, and step away from the screen.
wait until the anger is gone, then decide what to do next.
keep playing; he can't be tempted past what he can bear.
games.why: the door comes with the temptation, not after it. and sometimes the door is simply leaving the room: flee.

practice: Look at the nearest door, or picture one.

Bring to mind one pull that keeps coming back, a screen, a habit, a sharp tongue, and find its door: the moment it starts, and the small move that walks you out, like standing up or one slow breath before you answer.
If you pray, you can rest on Paul's four words: God is faithful.

wordCard.voice: A way of escape. Paul's promise that alongside the temptation God makes a door, so it can be borne.

orig.note: Greek: a way out. the KJV has a way to escape.

carryVoice: The line to keep: a way to escape, built right into the moment you need it. Day done.
